status_summary: As of 2026-10-21 the 2022 borrower defense and closed school discharge rules (effective July 2023) remain sidelined by statute rather than by ED rulemaking: per the Congressional Research Service, section 85001 of Public Law 119-21 (signed 2025-07-04) provides that for loans originated before 2035-07-01 the 2023 regulations are not in effect and the earlier rules apply. ED's PSLF rule (published 2025-10-31, effective date 2026-07-01), which would have let ED deny qualifying-employer status to employers found to have a substantial illegal purpose, was held contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority by the District of Massachusetts on 2026-06-30 and was vacated that day by that court and the District of Columbia (CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11472); ED appealed both judgments on 2026-08-27 and on 2026-09-22 published a Federal Register notice removing the employer attestation from the PSLF form to comply with the vacatur. On 2026-07-17 the Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of ED's motion to modify the Sweet borrower defense class settlement. PSLF itself remains in place under the 2025 law and ED's 2026-05-01 loan rule, and no bill ending PSLF or limiting the Secretary's cancellation authority, and no ED rulemaking rescinding the 2022 rules, was located as of 2026-10-21.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14235, Restoring Public Service Loan Forgiveness, is signed (the White House page dates it 2025-03-07; ED's 2025-10-31 rule, below, gives the order number). It directs ED to propose revisions to the PSLF regulation so that organizations with a substantial illegal purpose, including aiding immigration violations, do not count as public service employers.

Public Law 119-21 is signed. CRS reports that section 85001 delays the 2022 borrower defense and closed school discharge rules so that, for loans originated before 2035-07-01, the 2023 regulations are not in effect and the prior rules apply, effective on enactment; the law's table of contents lists separate headings for sections 85001 and 85002. CRS also reports that section 82004 counts payments under the new Repayment Assistance Plan as qualifying PSLF payments and that the Act does not otherwise change PSLF. A March 2026 complaint by school-sector plaintiffs describes the same 2035 date and the revival of the 2019 provisions.

ED publishes a final PSLF rule amending 34 CFR 685.219 so that employers with a substantial illegal purpose (including aiding violations of federal immigration law and certain procedures on minors) can be excluded from qualifying employer status, effective 2026-07-01.

The Ninth Circuit, in Sweet v. McMahon (No. 26-1136), denies ED's emergency motion to stay, pending appeal, the settlement deadline for deciding borrower defense applications from post-class applicants, finding ED had not shown it was likely to prove that the district courts abused their discretion in declining to modify the settlement; the court sets expedited briefing.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (order)

timeline.event: ED publishes final regulations implementing the loan provisions of Public Law 119-21 (new loan limits, Repayment Assistance Plan, phase-out of other income-driven plans), effective 2026-07-01; they clarify that Repayment Assistance Plan payments can qualify for PSLF. The portions read did not address borrower defense or closed school discharge.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (Judge Myong Joun), in a memorandum of decision in the consolidated challenges brought by nonprofit groups and by states (Nos. 25-cv-13242 and 25-cv-13244), holds ED's PSLF rule contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority, because the statute defines public service jobs and the general rulemaking provisions ED cited do not allow it to add an exclusion for employers with a substantial illegal purpose. The same day the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (No. 25-cv-03860), in a suit by 501(c)(3) organizations, held the statute requires credit for full-time work at any 501(c)(3) organization; per CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11472 both courts vacated the rule the day before its effective date. The copies of the Massachusetts memorandum read end before its remedy section.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

timeline.event: The Ninth Circuit, in an unpublished memorandum in Sweet v. McMahon (No. 26-1136), affirms the district court's denial of ED's Rule 60(b) motion to modify the Sweet borrower defense class settlement, finding no abuse of discretion because ED knew of the post-class applicant population when it agreed to the settlement. A law-firm litigation summary reports that the mandate issued on 2026-09-08 and that class counsel moved on 2026-08-18 to enforce the settlement, with a hearing set for 2026-11-05.

title: Curb student loan forgiveness: borrower defense, PSLF, and closed-school rules
uncertainties: The operative text of sections 85001 and 85002 could not be read in this review: the govinfo.gov HTML of Public Law 119-21 was re-opened on 2026-10-22 and stops within Title I, and congress.gov could not be opened. The readable table of contents lists section 85001 as the delay of the borrower defense rule and section 85002 as the delay of the closed school discharge rules, with PSLF treatment in section 82004. An external retrieval of the official enrolled text (not verified against an opened copy) reports that each section applies from enactment to loans first originated before 2035-07-01, that the borrower defense regulations that took effect on 2020-07-01 are restored and the prior closed school provisions apply, and that neither section changes PSLF or repayment plans. CRS attributes both delays to section 85001, so that attribution appears to be a simplification (inference); the 2035-07-01 date and the effect of the delay otherwise come from the CRS report (R48727) as read in summary form in an earlier review. CRS says the prior rules apply and that ED processes applications under pre-2023 standards left in place by court stays; the 'revival of the 2019 provisions' wording comes from the plaintiffs' March 2026 complaint in Career Colleges & Schools of Texas v. ED. The District of Massachusetts memorandum of 2026-06-30 (Doc. 127 in No. 25-cv-13242, Doc. 113 in No. 25-cv-13244) was opened on the courtlistener storage host and on the Massachusetts attorney general's site, but the retrievable text stops before the remedy section, so the vacatur sentence and the rulings on the arbitrary-and-capricious and First Amendment claims were not read; the vacatur rests on CRS. The District of Columbia opinion (No. 25-cv-03860, ECF 47) was found only on a party-side file host that is not used as a source, so the District of Columbia ruling also rests on CRS and on counsel's litigation page on citizen.org, which says the rule was vacated and the Department appealed. An external retrieval reported First Circuit Nos. 26-1972 and 26-1973 and D.C. Circuit No. 26-5308, and that joint stipulations dismissed Nos. 26-1972 and 26-5308 on 2026-10-21 with No. 26-1973 pending; no appellate order or docket was opened, so these reports are unverified and are not reflected in the timeline or court_status. The law-firm summaries differ slightly on grounds (Orrick adds statutory, arbitrary and capricious and First Amendment grounds for Massachusetts; CRS describes statutory grounds for both). Whether ED has opened rulemaking to formally rescind the 2022 rules after the suspension, and the end of the COVID payment pause (Mandate p. 340), were not verified beyond a Federal Register search of ED documents that showed no such rulemaking. Freshness check on 2026-10-21: a Federal Register search of ED documents published from 2026-08-27 found no borrower defense, closed school discharge or PSLF rulemaking; the only PSLF item was the 2026-09-22 form notice, which prints the executive order number and the proposed rule's date inconsistently with ED's 2025-10-31 rule. The Ninth Circuit orders in Sweet were read directly; the 2026-09-08 mandate, the 2026-08-18 enforcement motion and the 2026-11-05 hearing still rest on a law-firm summary. A plaintiffs' brief in Career Colleges & Schools of Texas v. ED (W.D. Tex.), hosted by a law firm, states that ED moved to dismiss on 2026-05-05 and suggested the 2022 rules might be rescinded in future; this is a party characterization, not an ED document.
